name: Puerto Rico
summary: A Caribbean island ruled by Spain from 1508 and by the United States since 1898; its people are US citizens (1917), and it became a self-governing Commonwealth in 1952 without becoming a US state.

knownFor.label: El Morro
knownFor.note: Spanish fortress in Old San Juan.

knownFor.label: Salsa and reggaeton
knownFor.note: Music with roots in Puerto Rico.

location.value: Between the Dominican Republic and the US Virgin Islands; about 9,100 km².

terrain.value: Mostly mountainous, crossed by the Cordillera Central; El Yunque is the only tropical rainforest in the US Forest Service system.

climate.value: Mostly tropical rainforest; warm to hot all year, with Atlantic hurricanes.

resources.value: Sugar and coffee in the past, and later manufacturing, pharmaceuticals and tourism.

disasters.value: Hurricanes Irma and Maria (2017) caused devastating damage, about $100 billion for Maria; a 6.4 earthquake struck in 2020.

population.value: About 3.2 million, and falling because of emigration and a low birth rate.

urbanisation.value: San Juan is the capital and most populous municipality, followed by others in its metropolitan area.

disease.value: Dengue has recurred, and the health system was badly strained after Hurricane Maria in 2017.

migration.value: From soon after World War II, waves of Puerto Ricans moved to the US mainland, especially the north-eastern states and Florida.

economicBase.value: Manufacturing (mainly pharmaceuticals, petrochemicals and electronics), then services such as tourism.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade is within the US customs area, with the port of San Juan as its hub.

wealth.value: Poorer than Mississippi, the poorest US state, but with the highest GDP per person in Latin America.

moneyAndTax.value: The US dollar; residents pay no federal income tax on local income.

inequality.value: Over a third of the population lives below the poverty line.

governmentType.value: A self-governing US territory (commonwealth); its constitution was approved in 1952.

keyRulers.value: Luis Muñoz Marín, first elected governor (1949).

institutions.value: A two-chamber Legislative Assembly; a nonvoting resident commissioner in the US Congress.

eliteConflict.value: Political status is an ongoing debate between statehood, independence and free association.

armyAndTech.value: US military bases; Vieques was used for naval bombing practice until 2003.

territoryChange.value: No change since 1898, when the island passed from Spain to the United States.

alliancesRivals.value: Part of the US system as a self-governing territory, with debate over statehood or independence.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; Puerto Rico is better known for its music and baseball players.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Puerto Rico, the largest and oldest university system, with 11 campuses.

openness.value: Open to US trade and migration, with large Puerto Rican communities on the US mainland.

communicationTransport.value: The Tren Urbano metro; Luis Muñoz Marín airport, the Caribbean’s largest air hub; San Juan, the Caribbean’s busiest port.

religion.value: Mainly Christian; Catholicism came with Spanish colonists.

artsArchitecture.value: Old San Juan, with Spanish colonial forts such as El Morro and San Cristóbal.

socialStructure.value: Mixed European, African and Indigenous (Taíno) ancestry.

sharedIdentity.value: A distinct Puerto Rican identity, fusing European, African and Indigenous elements, emerged by the late 19th century.

dailyLife.value: Cuisine rooted in Spanish, African and Taíno cooking.

ideasReligions.value: An ongoing debate over political status: statehood, independence or free association.

peakPeriod.value: From the mid-20th century, US and local economic projects worked to industrialise the island.

declineSignals.value: A government-debt crisis (2016–17) and population loss of about half a million in the 21st century.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
